title: O(n log n) Mixing Time Conjecture for Glauber Dynamics
statement_text: The Glauber dynamics for $k$-colourings of a graph $G$ with maximum degree $\Delta$ has mixing time $O(n \log n)$, provided that $k \geq \Delta + 2$.
context_text: Described as 'a famous conjecture in the area' in the introduction. Jerrum and independently Salas and Sokal proved rapid mixing for $k \geq 2\Delta$; Vigoda improved this to $k \geq 11\Delta/6$. The paper asks whether this $O(n \log n)$ bound can be extended to Glauber dynamics for $(\Delta+1)$-colourings restricted to the non-frozen component, and Proposition 3 answers in the negative for constant $\Delta$.
paper_contribution: Proves (Proposition 3) that the mixing time of Glauber dynamics for $(\Delta+1)$-colourings restricted to the non-frozen component can be at least $n^2/(8(\Delta+1))$, showing the $O(n\log n)$ bound cannot be extended to $k = \Delta+1$.
notes: No formal theorem environment; stated as 'a famous conjecture in the area' in prose without an explicit attributed citation label. PDF source.

title: Informal: Δ = o(n) condition not necessary for Corollary 2
statement_text: In the statement 'for every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with maximum degree $\Delta=o(n)$, Glauber dynamics for $(\Delta+1)$-colourings of $G$ started at a uniformly random $(\Delta+1)$-colouring gives an almost uniform sampler for random $(\Delta+1)$-colourings', the condition $\Delta=o(n)$ is probably not necessary.
context_text: Let $G$ have $n$ vertices and maximum degree $\Delta$. A $(\Delta+1)$-colouring is a proper colouring with colours in $[\Delta+1]$; it is frozen if every colour appears in the closed neighbourhood of every vertex, so that no single vertex can be recoloured. Glauber dynamics for $k$-colourings is the Markov chain on proper $k$-colourings that at each step picks a vertex $v$ and a colour $c\in[k]$ uniformly at random and recolours $v$ with $c$ if no neighbour of $v$ has colour $c$. For $k=\Delta+1$ frozen colourings are fixed points, and Feghali, Johnson and Paulusma showed that for $\Delta\ge3$ they are the only obstruction: the recolouring graph consists of one component containing all non-frozen colourings plus isolated frozen colourings. The authors' main theorem: if $3\le\Delta\le n-2$ and $G$ is connected, a uniformly random $(\Delta+1)$-colouring $\alpha$ satisfies $\Pr(\alpha\text{ is frozen})\le(6/7)^{n/(\Delta+1)}$ (the conditions are needed, e.g. every $(\Delta+1)$-colouring of $K_{\Delta+1}$ is frozen). The authors deduce the sampling statement: when $\Delta=o(n)$, the probability of starting at a frozen colouring is $o(1)$ and frozen colourings contribute $o(1)$ to the stationary distribution, so the chain converges to the uniform distribution on the non-frozen component, which is close in total variation to the uniform distribution on all $(\Delta+1)$-colourings. They remark right after that the condition $\Delta=o(n)$ is probably not necessary. The remark is informal: the paper does not say which weaker condition is intended (some condition is needed, since all colourings of $K_{\Delta+1}$ are frozen).
notes: Stated in running prose immediately after Corollary 2: 'The condition Δ = o(n) is probably not necessary.' PDF source.

title: Informal: Exponent in Theorem 1 not optimal
statement_text: The dependence on $\Delta$ in the exponent of the bound $\Pr(\alpha\text{ is frozen})\le(6/7)^{n/(\Delta+1)}$, valid for every connected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with maximum degree $\Delta$, $3\le\Delta\le n-2$, and a uniformly random $(\Delta+1)$-colouring $\alpha$ of $G$, is not best possible.
context_text: Let $G$ have $n$ vertices and maximum degree $\Delta$. A $(\Delta+1)$-colouring is a proper colouring with colours in $[\Delta+1]$; it is frozen if every colour appears in the closed neighbourhood of every vertex, so that no single vertex can be recoloured. Glauber dynamics for $k$-colourings is the Markov chain on proper $k$-colourings that at each step picks a vertex $v$ and a colour $c\in[k]$ uniformly at random and recolours $v$ with $c$ if no neighbour of $v$ has colour $c$. For $k=\Delta+1$ frozen colourings are fixed points, and Feghali, Johnson and Paulusma showed that for $\Delta\ge3$ they are the only obstruction: the recolouring graph consists of one component containing all non-frozen colourings plus isolated frozen colourings. The authors' main theorem: if $3\le\Delta\le n-2$ and $G$ is connected, a uniformly random $(\Delta+1)$-colouring $\alpha$ satisfies $\Pr(\alpha\text{ is frozen})\le(6/7)^{n/(\Delta+1)}$ (the conditions are needed, e.g. every $(\Delta+1)$-colouring of $K_{\Delta+1}$ is frozen). On the other hand, for every $n_0$ and every $\Delta\ge3$ there are $n\ge n_0$ and a connected $\Delta$-regular graph on $n$ vertices with $\Pr(\alpha\text{ is frozen})\ge e^{-\frac{3\log\Delta}{\Delta}n}$; this is only a factor $\log\Delta$ off in the exponent from the upper bound, and the authors believe the upper bound's dependence on $\Delta$ can be improved. These examples contain many cliques of size $\Delta$; the authors also show that $\Delta$-regular graphs of arbitrarily large girth can have frozen colourings, while a uniformly random $\Delta$-regular graph has a frozen colouring with probability at most $e^{-cn}$.
